Harm
harm
noun
Old English hearm, injury, hurt, evil. A plain and ancient word for real damage done to body, soul, or estate. In recent therapeutic and activist usage 'harm' has been inflated far beyond injury to cover discomfort, disagreement, and exposure to unwelcome truth — 'words are violence,' 'that's harmful.'

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
A real category inflated until truth and correction count as harm; faithful wounds are a kindness, not an injury.

📖 Biblical Definition

Harm in its true sense is a real and serious category. The believer is to 'do no murder,' to love his neighbor as himself, and so to work 'no ill to his neighbour' (Rom. 13:10); the law protects life, body, and property from genuine injury (Exod. 21-22). The wicked 'imagine mischief' and 'their feet run to evil... wasting and destruction are in their paths' (Isa. 59:7). Doing harm — actual injury to a neighbor's life, body, name, or goods — is forbidden, and protecting the weak from it is a duty (Ps. 82:3-4). But Scripture measures harm by God's law, not by subjective offense, and it knows that the deepest wounds are sometimes the most loving: 'faithful are the wounds of a friend' (Prov. 27:6); 'open rebuke is better than secret love' (Prov. 27:5). A truth that stings is not therefore a harm; often it is the very kindness a soul most needs (Ps. 141:5).

📜 Origin & Era

A real category (do no harm) inflated until disagreement, correction, or biblical truth itself counts as 'harm' or 'violence,' recasting the faithful as aggressors.

HARM, noun. Injury or hurt to body, soul, name, or estate; real damage done to a neighbor.

From Old English hearm, injury, evil — a plain word for genuine injury.

Legitimate use: Scripture forbids doing ill to a neighbor (Rom. 13:10) and commands protecting the weak from injury (Ps. 82:3-4).

Corrupt use: inflated to cover discomfort, disagreement, or unwelcome truth — 'words are violence' — so that telling the truth becomes 'doing harm.'

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 13:10 — "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."

Proverbs 27:6 — "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful."

Proverbs 27:5 — "Open rebuke is better than secret love."

Psalm 141:5 — "Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities."

Galatians 4:16 — "Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A real category — do no harm — is inflated until disagreement, correction, or biblical truth itself counts as 'harm' or even 'violence,' turning the faithful witness into the aggressor.

expand to see more

The corruption is the swelling of a true word until it bursts its meaning. 'Harm' properly names real injury — murder, theft, slander, abuse — and the Christian is bound to do none of it (Rom. 13:10). But in therapeutic and activist usage the word is stretched to cover any experience a person finds distressing: to be disagreed with is 'harm,' to be corrected is 'harm,' to hear that there are two sexes or that Christ is the only way (John 14:6) is 'harm,' and at the extreme, 'words are violence.' Once any unwelcome truth qualifies as harm, the one who speaks it is automatically the wrongdoer, and the door to faithful witness is closed in the name of compassion. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the inflated 'harm/violence' usage is named here to rebut it. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: 'harmful' as subjective-distress category is named to rebut it.

Scripture refuses this inflation by measuring harm against God's law rather than against feeling, and by insisting that loving wounds are not harms at all. 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend' (Prov. 27:6); the righteous man welcomes a reproof as 'an excellent oil' (Ps. 141:5). Paul asks the Galatians, 'Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?' (Gal. 4:16) — exposing the very logic the inflated word relies on: that the truth-teller has become the assailant. A surgeon's knife is not an assault; a watchman's warning is not an attack; a faithful rebuke is not abuse. To call them 'harm' is to mistake the cure for the disease.

The recovery holds both halves: take real harm with deadly seriousness, and refuse to let the word be counterfeited. The church must be the fiercest enemy of actual injury — it must defend the abused, the slandered, the genuinely wounded (Ps. 82:3-4), and never hide behind 'truth-telling' to excuse cruelty, for the manner of truth is to be spoken 'in love' (Eph. 4:15). But it must also refuse the redefinition that makes obedience itself an offense. Discomfort is not damage; conviction is not violence; the truth that wounds to heal (Hos. 6:1) is the opposite of harm. Love works no ill to its neighbor — and the greatest ill would be to leave him in a lie.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English hearm, real injury; a true category inflated until truth and correction count as 'harm' or 'violence.' Scripture measures harm by God's law and calls faithful wounds a kindness, not a harm.

Old English: hearm, injury, hurt, evil — a plain word for genuine damage to body, soul, name, or goods.

Biblical measure: Rom. 13:10, love 'worketh no ill' — harm gauged by God's law, not by subjective offense.

The loving wound: Prov. 27:6 and Ps. 141:5 — a faithful rebuke is 'a kindness' and 'excellent oil,' the opposite of harm.
